page10_img_1.png.title: CLUSTERCHANGES workflow: cluster, author-validate, tag partitions for reviewers
page10_img_1.png.description: A left-to-right workflow diagram showing how a submitted changeset is processed by CLUSTERCHANGES. On the left an author’s changeset is depicted as multiple document icons with colored diff highlights; an engine labeled “Cluster Changes” (step 1) groups those diff-regions into separate boxes (partitions). The middle shows the author again with the grouped partitions and green checkmarks (step 2) indicating author inspection/approval; an arrow then leads to a larger structured package where partitions are labeled/tagged (e.g., “@refactoring”, “@bugfix”) (step 3). A reviewer icon at the right receives the organized, tagged partitions — illustrating the paper’s intended flow: automatic decomposition, author review of partitions (steps 1–2 addressed in this work), and ordering/tagging for reviewer consumption (future work).

page4_img_1.png.title: CLUSTERCHANGES tree view with linked diff highlighting
page4_img_1.png.description: Screenshot of the CLUSTERCHANGES prototype showing the partitioned tree (left) and the linked textual diff view (right). The tree is headed “Partitions” and lists two non-trivial partitions (one highlighted in red, one in orange) with files and an enclosing method (e.g., Binder_Conversions.cs → MemberGroupFinalValidationAccessibilityChecks(...)) and a collapsed “Trivial Partitions” group containing Binder_Expressions.cs. The right pane displays the corresponding source lines (487–500) with diff highlighting (red for removed lines, green for added lines, yellow for modified contexts) and a green outline indicating the currently selected diff-region, illustrating how a partition selection maps to specific diff-regions in the code.

page7_img_1.png.title: Separated diff-regions: Regex change and corresponding test-string update
page7_img_1.png.description: A two-part code diff showing removed (red) and added (green) lines in two different classes. In MarkupHandler, the Regex initializer listRe is changed (old pattern with a digit prefix replaced by a pattern using ‘#’), while in MarkupTest the test string testStr is changed from "1. this is a test" to "#. this is a test". The snippet also shows MarkupList using listRe and MarkupTest calling MarkupHandler.MarkupList(testStr), so the regex change and the test update are semantically related via that method call; because MarkupList itself was not modified, CLUSTERCHANGES did not connect these two diff-regions, illustrating a missed use-use relationship.

page5_img_2.png.title: Histogram of trivial in-method partitions per review (1000 reviews)
page5_img_2.png.description: Bar chart (x-axis: number of trivial in-method partitions, 0–20; y-axis: number of reviews, up to 200) showing the distribution across 1000 changesets. Most reviews have very few trivial partitions: the mode is at 1 trivial partition (≈170–180 reviews), with secondary peaks at 2 and 3 (≈150 and ≈120 reviews respectively), and counts falling steadily for larger numbers. The distribution has a long right tail: by the 12–20 range counts are in the single digits, and the figure notes that about 4% of reviews have more than 20 trivial partitions (the paper additionally reports an extreme case with 326 trivial partitions). This indicates that while most changesets contain only a small number of trivial in-method partitions, a non-negligible minority contain many such trivial partitions.

page5_img_1.png.title: Distribution of non-trivial partitions per review (1000 changesets)
page5_img_1.png.description: Histogram (from 1000 Office changesets) showing how many non-trivial partitions each review contains. The modal bin is 1 non-trivial partition (~45–47% of reviews); combining 0 and 1 yields ~58% of reviews (the set the authors manually examined). Reviews with 2–5 non-trivial partitions account for about 40% (the pool used for the user study), while reviews with six or more partitions are rare (~1.4%), producing a steeply declining tail as the partition count increases.

page2_img_2.png.title: Boxplots of files, methods, and diff‑regions per changeset
page2_img_2.png.description: Three adjacent vertical boxplots summarize the distribution (from a 1000‑review sample) of: files changed (left), methods changed (center), and diff‑regions (right). The center lines show medians of roughly 4–5 files, 12 methods, and 24 diff‑regions; the method and diff‑region plots have substantially larger interquartile ranges and long right tails with many high outliers (axes reach ≈30, 50, and 100 respectively). These skewed distributions — with over 25% of reviews changing ~23 methods and ~45 diff‑regions as noted in the text — illustrate that a nontrivial fraction of reviews are large and composed of many scattered edit regions, motivating the need for automated decomposition.

page2_img_1.png.title: Diff excerpt from BinderFactoryVisitor showing two added code regions
page2_img_1.png.description: A code-review diff of BinderFactory.BinderFactoryVisitor.cs (lines ~447–461) showing two green-highlighted added regions separated by unchanged lines. The first added block (around line 450) inserts an if-check that calls VisitCore(...), while the second block (around lines 455–461) adds a return to VisitPropertyOrIndexerExpressionBody(parent) and introduces a private Binder VisitPropertyOrIndexerExpressionBody(...) with a call to CreateBinderCacheKey. In the paper this snippet is used to illustrate def-use relationships: the call added at ~450 refers to a method introduced in another file in the same changeset, whereas the call added near ~455 refers to the helper method defined immediately below (line ~458), which makes the inter-file versus in-file relationships explicit for CLUSTERCHANGES’ partitioning.
